rationale:
Today's slate stays inside the plague focus and doesn't repeat any angle from Oct 7. That rules out the status-decoder long-form, the 3-forms carousel, and the Shorts on person-to-person spread, curability and US cases.

**Mix**
- **Rising (S1, C1):** what happens after exposure, and what agencies actually say about risk. These match what people are searching now.
- **Emerging (S2):** CDC traveler monitoring, which broke Oct 7 and has almost no creator explainers yet.
- **Evergreen with a timely hook (L1):** Madagascar 2017, tied to the Irkutsk contacts nearing the end of monitoring.
- **Contrarian but true (S3):** there is no licensed plague vaccine for the public in the US; antibiotics and public-health measures are the main tools.

**Traffic and pillars**
- S1 is a spin-off of L1 and drives traffic to it.
- Pillars rotate across outbreaks (2 pieces, the maximum), news decoded, treatment and prevention, and risk/myth-correction.

**Playbook formats used**
- Plain-question titles that put "Plague" first.
- One dated, attributed number at most per title.
- An action framing modelled on the anaesthesia Short.
- No fear words.

**Playlists:** every piece uses the `general` pillar key ("Health Science Explained"). The playlist list we were given only has GLP-1 playlists, so none of them fit plague content.

**Caution and accuracy rules**
- **Caution topics:** S1 and C1 come from topics the radar marked caution. They use only attributed, dated agency statements.
- **Status wording:** everything says "suspected" or "reported", and "not confirmed isn't ruled out".
- **Preventive antibiotics:** always described as given by health authorities, never as self-treatment.
- **Excluded:** the peaking, politically charged embassy-alert topic, and anything about bioweapons or leaks.

pieces.topic: Madagascar 2017: how a large urban pneumonic plague outbreak was stopped with contact tracing, preventive antibiotics given by health authorities, and treatment centres. Tied to the Irkutsk contacts now finishing monitoring.
pieces.angle: Same structure. Hook: 'In Irkutsk, a lab worker died of pneumonia. Media reported it as suspected pneumonic plague. Russian authorities say the cause is unknown and that no dangerous pathogens were found in her 197 reported contacts. Rospotrebnadzor reported that over 90% had finished monitoring (as of Oct 7, 2026). WHO says the cause is not yet known. Not confirmed isn't ruled out.' Madagascar totals from a single dated WHO report (e.g. 2,348 cases, 202 deaths, 1 Aug–22 Nov 2017, WHO DON 27 Nov 2017), with its confirmed/probable/suspected split. Title: 'How Madagascar Brought Pneumonic Plague Under Control in 2017 (and What It Means Now)'.
pieces.working_title: How Madagascar Stopped Pneumonic Plague in 2017 (and What It Means Now)
pieces.why: Evergreen depth piece with a timely hook (Irkutsk contacts finishing monitoring). Few creators cover it in depth, and it backs the calm, expert line that global spread is unlikely. | fact-check: Good evergreen case study, but the status line needs fixing. Verified: on Oct 6, 2026 WHO said Russian authorities told it that no dangerous pathogens were found in any contact, and none had symptoms (UN Geneva newsroom, WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier: https://www.unognewsroom.org/story/en/3289/irkutsk-suspected-plague-death-who). Rospotrebnadzor calls the death 'pneumonia of unknown aetiology'. As of Oct 8, WHO (Maria Van Kerkhove) says the cause is still not known (Al Jazeera: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/8/russia-dismisses-reports-of-second-plague-case-as-false-information). The '197 contacts' figure is reported by several outlets. The 'over 90% completed monitoring' figure comes from Rospotrebnadzor (it was 60% on Oct 5), so credit Rospotrebnadzor as reported by the outlet, not Euronews alone. I couldn't open a Euronews Oct 7 page that says this; re-check before publishing. Madagascar: WHO DON of 27 Nov 2017 gives 2,348 confirmed, probable and suspected cases and 202 deaths (CFR 8.6%), 1 Aug–22 Nov 2017 (https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/27-november-2017-plague-madagascar-en). WHO AFRO's later update gives 2,384 cases and 207 deaths to 24 Nov. Pick one dated WHO report and don't mix the two. Keep the WHO split of confirmed, probable and suspected cases, which supports section 4. Don't mention the unverified second-case media reports, which the Kremlin calls false and WHO is asking about, beyond 'WHO has asked Russia for more information'. 'Stopped' is acceptable if you cite WHO's end-of-outbreak statement. Otherwise say 'brought under control'.

pieces.topic: Possible plague exposure? What health authorities do next: identify close contacts, monitor them, give preventive antibiotics, isolate anyone with symptoms
pieces.angle: 35–50 s. Open: 'Think you might have been exposed to plague? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Don't self-treat or stockpile antibiotics.' Then 4 steps: health authorities trace close contacts, monitor them (CDC wording), give preventive antibiotics to close contacts where they decide it's needed, and isolate and treat anyone with symptoms. Status line: 'Irkutsk: plague suspected in media reports, not confirmed. Russian authorities report pneumonia of unknown cause; Rospotrebnadzor says over 90% of 197 contacts have finished monitoring (as of Oct 7, 2026).' Close: 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
pieces.working_title: Possible Plague Exposure? What Health Authorities Do Next #shorts
pieces.target_keyword: what happens if exposed to plague
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1: the contact-tracing playbook in 45 seconds, pointing to the Madagascar long-form. Action-framed titles got 57 for us, and the contact count is the most concrete fact in the story. | fact-check: Good action Short that fits the playbook. Fix the status line: Russian authorities officially call this pneumonia of unknown cause, and WHO says on Oct 8 that the cause is not yet known. 'Suspected, not confirmed' is fine only if the Short also says officials haven't confirmed plague and are reporting no dangerous pathogens in contacts. Credit the 197 contacts and 'over 90% monitored' to Rospotrebnadzor (as reported), dated Oct 7, 2026, and re-check before publishing. Step 3 must say health authorities decide on and give preventive antibiotics to close contacts, so it can't read as 'contacts should take antibiotics'. Take the incubation and monitoring wording from a reachable CDC plague page and quote it word for word. cdc.gov/plague/faq/ returned 404, so link the specific live page.

pieces.topic: Why the CDC is monitoring travelers arriving from Siberia: port health stations, symptom screening and what a returning traveler should do
pieces.angle: 35–50 s. Open: 'CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the US risk from the unconfirmed case is extremely low (Reuters, Oct 7, 2026). Monitoring arrivals is a precaution.' Explain the port health stations (e.g. JFK) and interagency screening. Action: 'Recently traveled and now have fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently and mention your travel.' Include the Yellow Book line only if a live CDC page confirms it. Close: 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
pieces.working_title: Why Is the CDC Monitoring Travelers From Siberia? #shorts
pieces.why: Broke Oct 7 (Axios, Reuters) with almost no creator explainers. It's a concrete, low-competition US-audience story with a recognisable subject in a question title. | fact-check: Verified via the Reuters story (syndicated: https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/cdc-sees-low-plague-risk-173012557.html): CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the risk to the US from an 'unconfirmed' pneumonic plague case is 'extremely low'. CDC is working with DHS, State and other agencies, and its JFK port health station can carry out surveillance and screening. Keep the word 'unconfirmed' and credit Reuters. Leave out the 'Department of War' mention and the suspended-flights context, because they pull toward politics. The Yellow Book line ('no plague in returning US travelers in more than 40 years') was reported for the 2024 edition. But wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/yellowbook/2024/infections-diseases/plague now redirects to a zoonotic-exposures page that doesn't contain the claim. Use it only if the scriptwriter finds a live CDC page that says it; otherwise drop it. Say 'Siberian region' or 'Irkutsk region' rather than broad Siberia framing, and add no commentary about Russia.

pieces.topic: Is there a plague vaccine? The live EV vaccine given to at-risk workers in former Soviet countries since the 1930s, vs no licensed plague vaccine for the general public in the US
pieces.angle: 35–50 s. Open: 'Is there a plague vaccine? In the US, CDC says no plague vaccine is available. Antibiotics and public-health measures are the main tools.' Then: 'Russia and some neighbouring countries use a live vaccine called EV, in use since the mid-1930s, mainly for people at high risk such as lab staff working with live plague cultures. It can cause strong reactions, and CDC says there isn't strong evidence that older vaccines protect against the pneumonic form.' No mention of the Irkutsk worker's vaccination. Close: 'Early antibiotics save lives. With possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Title: 'Is There a Plague Vaccine? The US vs Russia #shorts'.
pieces.working_title: Is There a Plague Vaccine? What Lab Workers Get #shorts
pieces.why: Contrarian-but-true slot. 'She was vaccinated' raises an obvious question almost no outlet has explained. Low competition, with a peer-reviewed review to build on. | fact-check: (1) CDC's wording is 'A plague vaccine is not available' in the US. Don't narrow it to 'for the general public', which suggests some people in the US can get one. CDC also says there isn't strong evidence that vaccines used elsewhere protect against pneumonic plague; keep that line. (2) EV: PMC reviews confirm the live EV NIIEG vaccine has been used since the mid-1930s in the former USSR and is still used in Russia and Kazakhstan. They also note it causes strong reactions and that use outside Russia has declined (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4317636/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6559729/). (3) Drop the line about the Irkutsk worker's vaccination. I couldn't find it in Euronews (its Oct 4 article doesn't mention it). Plague isn't confirmed in her case, so the line would suggest a vaccine failure that hasn't been shown, and it puts the person who died at the centre. (4) The title 'What Lab Workers Get' suggests US lab workers get a vaccine. Change it.

pieces.topic: How worried should you be? The plague risk levels WHO and CDC have actually stated, and what a risk assessment weighs
pieces.angle: Slide 1: 'Russia plague report: what agencies say the risk is (as of Oct 8, 2026). Suspected in media reports, not confirmed. Russian authorities report pneumonia of unknown cause; WHO says the cause isn't yet known. Not confirmed isn't ruled out.' Slide 2: WHO initial risk assessment, quoted exactly with its 3 regions (WHO spokesperson, Oct 6). Slide 3: CDC 'extremely low' for the US (Director Erica Schwartz, Reuters, Oct 7). Keep slides 4–7 as planned, with a qualifier and a source tag on every cell, no agency hashtags and no doom words.
pieces.working_title: Russia Plague Report: What WHO and CDC Say the Risk Is (as of Oct 7)
pieces.target_keyword: should i be worried about plague
pieces.why: 'Should you be worried?' headlines are everywhere, and the CDC director's statement landed Oct 7. The attributed-number format performs near our median, and it works as a reference card people save. | fact-check: I checked WHO's primary statement (UN Geneva newsroom, Oct 6, 2026, spokesperson Christian Lindmeier). Exact wording: 'The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region.' Keep 'initial' and 'from the information available'. Credit it to the WHO spokesperson, not 'WHO statement' in general and not hromadske. CDC: Director Erica Schwartz via Reuters, Oct 7, 'extremely low' risk to the US from an 'unconfirmed' case. Slide 1 also needs the official Russian position (pneumonia of unknown cause, no dangerous pathogens found in contacts) and WHO's Oct 8 statement that the cause is not yet known. Don't repeat the second-case media reports. Slide 4: take 'close contact' from a live CDC plague page and quote it exactly. Every risk cell gets a qualifier: 'initial assessment, Oct 6' or 'US only, Oct 7'.
